title: Help: too many unique codes to uniquely identify locations
html:
Over the years, I feel like I have heard all kinds of names used for geographical identifiers in humanitarian environments. And, that includes many of the letters of the (English) alphabet - geographic (g), municipal (m), name (n) and so forth. In the end, the one that seems to have become the most well known is the place code - aka P-code - which came about years ago through an inter-agency effort to help with data exchange efforts. Yet, many organizations have continued to use or build their own unique codes. Experiences with P-codes show that they do not work for all mandates and missions, but coding geographical boundaries and providing interoperable data can bring great benefits to humanitarian and development interventions.

Earlier this year, the person perhaps most authoritative on P-codes - Tom Haythornthwaite - approached me to see if we could join forces to look at the P-codes, their history and their potential future. We teamed up with Elaine Donderer who led the research efforts leading to our new paper: Identifying places - Improving data connectivity through unique identifiers.

[PDF]

The paper hopes to encourage and to aid information managers and humanitarians in developing a joint system for identifying places. It covers the evolution of coding systems for geospatial boundaries and associated P-code attributes, discusses the barriers and experiences of professionals in the field, and explores potential future directions when considering emerging technologies.

The paper also touches on recommendations. Perhaps one of the most obvious is the need for some kind of universal adapter between the various organizational standards. As noted by Dr. Prashant Madhukar Hedao from the WHO GIS Centre for Health:

“We do not have a standardized electric plug across the world. You need an adapter to make sure you do not get into trouble. We are now at a point when it is too late to change all the plugs – the only solution is traveling with a universal adapter. The same goes for unique identifiers. This is why we should be careful in expanding on different unique identifiers. We need to make sure this is set up in an interoperable manner with inter-agency standards to ease information management and create an adapter for all kinds of data needs.”

Elaine, Tom and I hope that the paper will spur the necessary conversation, encourage organizations to collaborate and support an information environment in which many organizations and relevant actors can contribute to and benefit from geographic information and improved data connectivity.

Andrej
teaser: A paper with Elaine Donderer on building a shared way to identify places, as organizations keep creating their own geographic codes.
seo_description: The paper Identifying places on P-codes, the evolution of geospatial coding systems, and a joint approach to unique identifiers for data connectivity.
